title: Trump Announces 100% Tariff on Generic Drug Imports Starting August 2028
excerpt: President Trump said generic pharmaceuticals will remain tariff-free for two years before facing rates of 100% and eventually 200%, in a push to reshore manufacturing to the U.S.
body:
President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the United States will impose a 100% tariff on all imported generic pharmaceuticals beginning August 1, 2028, escalating to 200% one year later. The move marks the most direct threat yet to India's $12.7 billion pharmaceutical export pipeline to the U.S.

"Effective August 1st, 2026, all Generic Drugs being brought into the United States will continue to have a TARIFF of ZERO PERCENT for a two year period of time, after which the TARIFF will be raised to 100% for a one year period of time, and 200% thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social, according to The Wall Street Journal.

A Two-Year Window Before the Hammer Falls

The phased timeline gives drugmakers a runway to shift production stateside—or face punishing duties. Trump framed the policy explicitly as reshoring incentive, writing that it comes "with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time."

The announcement ends more than a year of internal administration debate. The Wall Street Journal reported that some White House staff had raised concerns about the tariff levels needed to reshore generic manufacturing, a notoriously low-margin business. Trump imposed tariffs on name-brand pharmaceuticals in April but explicitly left generics out at the time.

India's Pharma Sector in the Crosshairs

India supplies nearly 47% of America's pharmaceutical requirements, according to Pharmexcil, the government-backed trade body. Four out of ten prescriptions filled in the U.S. come from Indian companies. The country exported $12.7 billion in pharmaceutical goods to the U.S. in 2024, making it India's largest industrial export category.

The companies most exposed are those with heavy U.S. revenue dependence. Jefferies estimates that Zydus Lifesciences and Dr Reddy's Laboratories draw roughly 45% and 43% of sales from the U.S., respectively. Sun Pharmaceutical Industries derives about 30% from the American market, though over half its U.S. sales come from patented drugs, somewhat reducing its generic tariff exposure.

The industry operates on margins as low as 5%, leaving far less buffer to absorb tariff costs compared with branded manufacturers' typical 30–50% margins.

Healthcare Costs and Supply Chain Risks

Generic drugs account for 90% of all U.S. prescription volume. Roughly 83% of the top 100 prescribed generics depend on imports, with antibiotics and antivirals among the most vulnerable categories.

Aaron Kesselheim, a professor at Harvard Medical School, has argued in Health Affairs that tariffs raising production costs could shrink margins to the point where manufacturers exit, worsening existing drug shortages. Nearly one in four Americans already skip doses or don't fill prescriptions due to cost, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation.

What's Next

Some Indian drugmakers have already begun expanding U.S. manufacturing footprints in anticipation. Nandini Piramal, chairperson of Piramal Pharma, told Reuters: "If companies want to pay higher prices in the U.S. to make in the U.S., we're very happy to help them do so."

The two-year zero-tariff window sets up a critical period for the global pharmaceutical supply chain. Companies must decide whether to invest billions in U.S. manufacturing capacity—a process that typically takes years—or risk facing duties that could make their products uneconomical. The Indian Pharmaceutical Alliance has signalled it will pursue bilateral negotiations, but whether diplomacy can blunt a tariff regime explicitly designed as a manufacturing ultimatum remains to be seen.
